items.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: And then Hal Smith, myself and Keith had made some trio albums together.

ctx.x: Okay. He’s done some arranging for you also?
Yes, he did the Bing Crosby album, the arrangements on that. And then Hal Smith, myself and Keith had made some trio albums together.
That takes a lot of piano playing, to do the trio thing, doesn’t it?

items.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: Well that was with Bobby Gordon and we just did a little, it wasn’t a tribute or anything.

ctx.x: I see you were in on a Condon memorial thing too? Eddie Condon?

Yeah. Well that was with Bobby Gordon and we just did a little, it wasn’t a tribute or anything. Eddie Condon was a kind of a catalyst for music that’s now just completely out of any of these jazz critics or these educators would not mention Eddie Condon. I mean they think he’s absolutely beneath them. It’s a guy who was a wonderful rhythm guitar player. He didn’t play any solos. What did he do? He drank himself crazy and he was just part of the times, but he was a wonderful catalyst. He brought together so many…
Harvard people and businessmen and that. But they liked it. They liked the sound. A lot of them, like John O’Hara, the novelist, and — he wrote Cannery Row.
